summary: A Mobbin video that reviews 1,460 onboarding flows across 986 apps and websites to ask what makes onboarding good and whether a product needs one at all. It finds that the average app has 25 onboarding screens and that some of the longest flows belong to some of the most successful apps, so it suggests shortness may never have been the point; getting people to the moment they feel the product's value (the aha moment) is. The strongest flows sell the outcome instead of listing features, ask a few personalization questions and then show what the answers unlocked, add delight to long flows, and teach in context with checklists, tooltips and empty-state nudges instead of pop-ups. It also covers paywalls inside onboarding, custom screens before the notification permission prompt, and splitting a sign-up form across screens, citing A/B results for several of these. For a design system this gives concrete onboarding patterns, empty-state and permission-primer components, and a reminder that some products (inspiration libraries, AI chat) may be best with little or no onboarding.
key_ideas: Short onboarding is not the point; the average app in the sample has 25 onboarding screens and some of the longest flows belong to successful apps.
Good onboarding follows sign up, set up, then the aha moment where the user feels the product's value.
Welcome screens work best when they sell the outcome by showing the product in action, not by listing features.
Letting people try the core experience before signing up goes a step further in selling the outcome, and the video rarely sees it in apps with AI features.
A human touch, such as a founder's note or a CEO video at the aha moment, makes the product feel made with intention.
The best flows add personalization and make it worth the user's time; only 7% of AI apps personalize during onboarding, and AI tools seem to let the product learn from use instead.
Allowing more than one answer to a goal question (multi-intent) and a conversational quiz tone both raised conversion in cited tests.
After a quiz, show what the answers unlocked: a personal plan, a date the goal will be reached, or a home page filled with relevant content.
22% of the sample shows a paywall during onboarding; some apps pair it with personalization, a one-time offer, a page of social proof, tailored plans or a playful design.
Long flows can feel short when there is always something going on, such as animations on loading and verification steps.
Teach in context instead of front-loading education: reassuring copy, tooltips, live password requirement checks and empty-state nudges.
A persistent onboarding checklist outperformed pop-ups and banners and stays available after the user dismisses the flow.
A custom screen before the system notification prompt, optionally previewing the notification, is common and said to raise accept rates.
Splitting a sign-up form across several screens raised conversions in one case, so added friction in one place can remove it elsewhere.
Culture matters: audiences differ in how much information density feels efficient, so successful flows cannot simply be copied.
The flows that stuck brought users to value quickly: sometimes by adding delight to a long flow, sometimes by letting users personalize, sometimes by getting out of the way.
Some products may not need onboarding at all: when the product speaks for itself (an inspiration library, an AI chat whose first prompt is the value), letting users in fast may be best.

rules.rule: Make welcome screens show the product in action and the outcome it delivers instead of a list of features.
rules.why: The best onboarding screens studied had this in common; Timehop's welcome screen shows the product in action, and Runkeeper's animation conveys what the app does without reading a word.
rules.evidence: [1:10] They're not listing features, they're selling the outcome

rules.rule: Consider letting people try the core experience before asking them to create an account.
rules.why: It goes a step further in selling the outcome; Elma lets you try the core experience before sign-up, which the video rarely sees in apps with AI features, and Duolingo has users complete a first lesson before creating an account.
rules.evidence: [1:32] It lets you try the core experience before you sign up

rules.rule: Let users pick more than one goal in onboarding goal questions instead of forcing a single choice.
rules.why: Headspace found users arrive with more than one pain point; allowing several goals led to a 10% increase in free trial conversion.
rules.evidence: [3:04] Headspace found out that their users come to their app with more than one pain point

rules.rule: Write onboarding quiz questions in a conversational tone.
rules.why: Dollar Shave Club's conversational quiz copy alone led to a 5% increase in subscriptions.
rules.evidence: [3:37] Dollar Shave Club tweaked the quiz copy to be more conversational

rules.rule: After a personalization quiz, show what the answers unlocked: a personal plan, the date the goal will be reached, or a home page already filled with matching content.
rules.why: Before the product is used it already feels like it will work (Endless, Byte Pal, Brilliant, Speak).
rules.evidence: [3:48] They actually show you what those answers unlocked

rules.rule: When onboarding asks personalization questions, make them worth the user's time by visibly using the answers, for example customizing recommendations right away.
rules.why: The best flows add personalization and make it worth your time; Tide asks two questions, customizes recommendations as you watch, then prompts sign-up.
rules.evidence: [2:33] add personalization into the flow, and they make it worth your time

rules.rule: When onboarding includes a paywall, consider recommending pricing plans tailored to the user's quiz answers.
rules.why: Grammarly's tailored plan recommendations led to almost a 20% increase in plan upgrades.
rules.evidence: [5:19] As for Grammarly, based on your quiz answers, they recommend tailored pricing plans

rules.rule: In a long onboarding flow, give often-overlooked steps such as loading and verification states smooth animation so something is always happening.
rules.why: Bump and Bipul keep long flows fun so they do not feel like a boring onboarding; the loved flows make long onboarding feel short.
rules.evidence: [6:14] Smooth animations on things like verification that rarely get special treatment

rules.rule: Don't front-load all education at the start of onboarding; explain dry concepts step by step with reassuring copy and tooltips that state the impact of each step.
rules.why: Cake Equity makes equity and vesting approachable so users feel someone is guiding them along the way.
rules.evidence: [6:46] some apps don't front-load all the education to you

rules.rule: Make password fields check off each requirement in real time as the user types.
rules.why: It removes a reason to get stuck and makes the experience feel effortless.
rules.evidence: [7:08] a password field that checks off requirements in real time as you type

rules.rule: Replace a blank first-use empty state with a small nudge in the right place, instead of guided tours or pop-ups.
rules.why: To-do apps do this well: no guided tours, no pop-ups, just a nudge in the right place.
rules.evidence: [7:22] Instead of giving users a blank empty state

rules.rule: Use a clear, persistent onboarding checklist instead of pop-ups and banners to guide new users through setup.
rules.why: Mural's switch to a six-step checklist drove a 10% relative increase in one-week retention, and checklists stay around after the user dismisses the initial flow.
rules.evidence: [7:35] Mural replaced pop-ups and banners with a clear six-step checklist

rules.rule: Show a custom screen explaining the benefit before triggering the system notification permission prompt, optionally previewing the notification the user would receive.
rules.why: Many apps do this and it reportedly improves accept rates significantly (Brilliant, Center).
rules.evidence: [7:55] a lot of apps show a custom screen before the notification pop-up

rules.rule: Consider splitting a sign-up form into multiple screens.
rules.why: House saw a 15% increase in conversions after doing so; added friction in one place can remove friction in another.
rules.evidence: [8:25] House split their sign-up form into multiple screens

rules.rule: Don't copy another product's onboarding without checking it fits your audience's culture and density expectations.
rules.why: Users in Eastern markets tend to be more comfortable with information-heavy interfaces, so what feels like clutter to one audience feels efficient to another.
rules.evidence: [8:49] which is partly why we can't just copy what worked

rules.rule: If the product delivers value on first use (an inspiration library, an AI chat's first prompt), let users in fast with little or no onboarding.
rules.why: Mobbin and AI chat apps speak for themselves (the first prompt is where users find value), so the video suggests the best experience may be to let users in fast without an onboarding that gets in their way.
rules.evidence: [9:32] maybe the best experience is just to let users get in fast

rules.rule: Design onboarding to bring users to value (the aha moment) quickly, and judge a flow by that rather than by its screen count.
rules.why: The average app has 25 onboarding screens and some of the longest flows belong to successful apps; what the flows that stuck had in common was bringing users to value quickly.
rules.evidence: [9:02] they brought users to value quickly

rules.rule: Consider a human touch in onboarding, such as a founder's note, a personal CEO message, or a message at the aha moment.
rules.why: Some apps skip the pitch and just feel human (One Year's handwritten founder note, Tinder's birthday acknowledgement, Airbnb's CEO video after a first listing); Basecamp's CEO note makes the product feel made with intention.
rules.evidence: [1:49] Some apps skip the pitch entirely and just feel human

rules.rule: Consider rewriting the sign-up screen as a pitch, with social proof such as logos beside the form.
rules.why: Sometimes selling the outcome is just a copy tweak: Superhuman turns a boring sign-up screen into a pitch with logos on the side.
rules.evidence: [1:43] sometimes it could just be a copy tweak like Superhuman

rules.rule: Consider letting users customize a visible part of the app during onboarding, such as a map style.
rules.why: Focus Flight's map style choice makes the app feel like yours before you start using it.
rules.evidence: [3:26] Focus Flight lets you choose your map style during onboarding

rules.rule: Add small, unflashy guidance through onboarding steps, such as a progress indicator or helpful microcopy.
rules.why: None of this is flashy, but it removes reasons to get stuck and makes the experience feel effortless.
rules.evidence: [7:13] Maybe it's a progress indicator, maybe it's microcopy

rules.rule: When onboarding ends in a paywall, consider showing value or social proof first, such as a ready personal plan with a goal date or a page of social proof.
rules.why: Timely shows a full page of social proof before its paywall, and the raccoon app emphasizes the value (your plan is ready, you will reach your goal by a date) before its paywall.
rules.evidence: [5:04] Timely does the same with a full page of social proof before showing the paywall

decisions.question: How should the first onboarding screens sell the product?

options.name: Product in action
options.effect: The welcome screen shows the product working instead of a feature list.
options.when: As in Timehop, on both mobile and desktop.

options.name: Animation on open
options.effect: People get a feel for what the app does without reading a word.
options.when: As in Runkeeper.

options.name: Try the core experience first
options.effect: People use the core experience before signing up.
options.when: As in Elma; rare for apps with AI features.

options.name: Sign-up screen as a pitch
options.effect: A copy tweak turns sign-up into a pitch, with logos as social proof.
options.when: As in Superhuman.

options.name: A human touch
options.effect: Skip the pitch and feel human, for example a founder's note with a handwritten signature.
options.when: As in One Year and Basecamp.

decisions.recommendation: Sell the outcome, not a list of features: the best onboarding screens studied had that in common.
decisions.evidence: [1:10] They're not listing features, they're selling the outcome

decisions.question: Does this product need an onboarding flow, and how long should it be?

options.name: No onboarding, get in fast
options.effect: Users land straight in the product and find value on first use.
options.when: The product speaks for itself, like Mobbin or AI chat apps where the first prompt is the value.

options.name: Short and sweet
options.effect: A couple of questions, visible customization, then a sign-up prompt.
options.when: As in Tide: two questions, recommendations customize, then a sign-up prompt.

options.name: Long but delightful
options.effect: Dozens of screens with animation, personalization and a first win that do not feel long.
options.when: As in Duolingo (60 screens before sign-up, including a first lesson) or Bipul (61 screens with animation and a personal plan), which do not feel long.

decisions.recommendation: There is no single right length; the flows that stuck brought users to value quickly, whether by adding delight to a long flow, letting users personalize, or getting out of the way. Maybe it all boils down to the product.
decisions.evidence: [8:53] I don't think there's one right or wrong way to design an onboarding flow

decisions.question: When should people be asked to create an account?

options.name: First, before anything else
options.effect: Sign up, set up the account, then reach the aha moment.
options.when: The pattern the video says the best onboarding seems to follow.

options.name: After trying the core experience
options.effect: Users feel the value (a first lesson, an AI result) before committing.
options.when: The core experience can run without an account, as in Elma and Duolingo.

options.name: After personalization
options.effect: Users answer questions, watch recommendations adapt, then get prompted to sign up.
options.when: As in Tide: two questions, recommendations customize, then a sign-up prompt.

decisions.evidence: [0:46] You sign up, set up your account, you hit the aha moment

decisions.question: How should first-time users learn the product?

options.name: Pop-ups, banners and guided tours
options.effect: Interruptive overlays that disappear once dismissed.
options.when: The approach Mural replaced; the source does not recommend it.

options.name: Persistent checklist
options.effect: A clear list of setup steps that stays around after the initial flow is dismissed.
options.when: Setup has several steps; Mural's six-step checklist raised one-week retention 10% relative.

options.name: Nudges in the empty state
options.effect: A blank screen instead shows a small hint in the right place.
options.when: First-use screens with nothing in them yet, as in to-do apps.

options.name: Reassuring copy and tooltips per step
options.effect: Dry concepts are explained where they come up, so users feel guided.
options.when: The domain is complex or unfamiliar, as in Cake Equity's equity and vesting.

decisions.recommendation: Prefer checklists and contextual nudges over pop-ups and tours: the source cites a retention lift for a checklist and says such small aids make the experience feel effortless.
decisions.evidence: [7:35] Mural replaced pop-ups and banners with a clear six-step checklist

decisions.question: Should onboarding ask personalization questions, and what should it do with the answers?

options.name: Ask nothing, let the product learn
options.effect: No up-front questions; the product adapts from use.
options.when: Typical of AI tools (only 7% of AI apps personalize during onboarding).

options.name: Quiz, then show what it unlocked
options.effect: A personal plan, a goal date or a pre-filled home page makes the product feel like it will work before use.
options.when: Answers change what the user sees, as in Endless, Byte Pal, Brilliant and Speak.

options.name: Let users customize the look
options.effect: The app feels like theirs before they start, such as picking a map style.
options.when: As in Focus Flight's map style picker.

decisions.recommendation: Make personalization worth the user's time, and show what the answers unlocked rather than just collecting them.
decisions.evidence: [3:48] They actually show you what those answers unlocked

options.name: No paywall in onboarding
options.effect: Users reach the product without a purchase step.
options.when: 22% of the sample shows a paywall during onboarding, so this is the more common choice [inferred].

options.name: Paywall after a quiz with a one-time offer
options.effect: The offer is meant to drive urgency right after personalization.
options.when: Used by an app auto-captioned as 'The site'.

options.name: Social proof page before the paywall
options.effect: A full page of social proof comes before the paywall.
options.when: Used by Timely.

options.name: Tailored plan recommendation
options.effect: Plans are recommended from quiz answers.
options.when: Grammarly; almost a 20% increase in plan upgrades.

options.name: Playful paywall

options.name: System prompt directly

options.when: Not discussed as a recommended choice.

options.name: Custom screen first
options.effect: A screen explains the benefit (for example, reminders to build a habit) before the system prompt.
options.when: Brilliant does this; said to improve accept rates significantly.

options.name: Custom screen with a notification preview
options.effect: The primer also teases the notification the user will receive.

decisions.question: Should the sign-up form be one screen or split across several?

options.name: Single screen
options.effect: All fields at once.
options.when: Not discussed as a recommended choice.

options.effect: Fewer fields per step; more steps overall.
options.when: House did this and saw a 15% increase in conversions.

process.detail: Identify where users actually feel the product's value (Airbnb: first booking; Netflix: watching a show; Mobbin: saving a screen to a collection) and design onboarding to get there.
If the product delivers value immediately, like an inspiration library or an AI chat's first prompt, let users in fast; otherwise choose how long the flow must be.
Open with the product in action, animation, a try-before-sign-up, or a sign-up screen rewritten as a pitch with social proof.
Make questions worth the user's time, allow more than one goal, write them conversationally, then show what the answers unlocked.
Add animation and delight to steps like loading and verification so a long flow does not feel long.
Use reassuring copy, tooltips, live form validation, empty-state nudges and a persistent checklist instead of front-loaded education or pop-ups.
Show a custom screen that explains, and optionally previews, notifications before the system prompt.

caveats: The video is by Mobbin and draws all flows from Mobbin's library; it promotes Mobbin's AI search for onboarding checklists, says onboarding flows are the second most searched on Mobbin, and uses Mobbin as an example of a product that needs no onboarding.

The description links case studies for Headspace, multi-intent queries, conversational tone and Dollar Shave Club (the link list is cut off); the transcript gives no sample sizes, durations or test conditions for any cited result (Headspace, Dollar Shave Club, Grammarly, Mural, House).
The link between long onboarding and success is observational: some of the longest flows belong to successful apps, which does not show that length causes success.

Several claims are hedged in the source: pre-permission screens 'apparently' improve accept rates with no figure, and mobile's extra permission and paywall screens only 'might explain' why web onboarding is 21% shorter.
The Eastern-markets density claim is stated without a source.

App names come from auto-captions and some are uncertain: 'Elma', 'Byte Pal' and 'Bipul' (the raccoon app, possibly the same product), 'The site' (an unnamed app pairing a quiz with a one-time offer), 'Timely', 'Center' and 'House'.
Published 2026-04-16; percentages describe the sample at that time.
One-time offers 'to drive urgency' are reported neutrally; the source does not discuss whether such tactics pressure users [inferred].

Sample figures differ: 1,460 flows across 986 apps and websites (title, description), 'over a thousand' flows (intro), and 900-plus apps and websites for the 22% paywall figure; the video does not say how they relate.
The video says the best onboarding follows sign up, set up, then the aha moment, yet several flows it praises (Duolingo, Tide, Elma) put the value before sign-up; it does not reconcile the two.
